messages.subject: Advice for data analysis on Distance
parts:
Hi everyone, 
I am attempting to analyse my data on Distance for the first time, however I am not sure whether I am using the correct approach.

Last winter I carried out a bird survey in a semi-natural and in a planted forest using point transect sampling and I collected data on four different species. None of these species however, reach the suggested number of observations for point transects (80-100).

Considering that my primary aim is to compare the density estimates of the two types of forest stand, I post-stratified using the stratum layer (plantation and semi-natural) and set the level of resolution of estimates to stratum (hopefully that is correct?).
Now, seeing that my data include different species, should I use species as covariate, or this is used only when we want to estimate density for each species? 
I hope this makes sense!

Thanks in advance,
Eleonora

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Advice for data analysis on Distance
parts:
Eleonora

Several questions:

  • you say your interest is in comparison of density between habitats.  If you took habitat types into consideration when you designed your study, allocating sufficient points to each habitat type, then you shouldn't need to post-stratify.  I presume you identified the habitat type of each point at the stratum level, correct?  Then simple stratification will produce the stratum-specific density estimates.
  • as I read your message, it seems you are not interested in species-specific density estimates, is that correct?  If you wish to produce habitat-specific avian density estimates (combined across species), then you need not incorporate species in the detection function, as pooling robustness can accommodate heterogeneity in detectability across species.

Let me know how much of this I have misunderstood.
